tier_reason: bench/README.md carries every quoted number (standard-benchmark geomean 0.57x C Lua 5.5 with the JIT, 1.8x without, LuaJIT 0.18x; Mandelbrot 0.20x, spectral-norm 0.33x, fannkuch-redux 0.49x, DeltaBlue 0.90x; M1 Pro 0.75x against Lua 5.4). The benchmark code is public (bench/standard_test.go, bench/suite_test.go, bench/standard/ with the Are We Fast Yet Lua port, agreement tests) with raw output bench/suite-results-amd64.txt checked in, and Go 1.27.1, -count 6, -ldflags=-funcalign=64, taskset -c 0-5 and the AMD Ryzen 9 9900X3D are stated, so A holds.

corrections.caveats: Not faster than LuaJIT: the same table puts LuaJIT at 0.18x C Lua 5.5 against Apogee's 0.57x, so LuaJIT is about 3x faster (derived from page data); the win is over PUC C Lua only. The C Lua 5.5 and LuaJIT rows were measured on 2026-09-25 at commit 3d3b49e and carried over, while the Apogee rows are from 2026-09-27 at commit 45b42e8, and the README says rows move by up to 10% between days. C Lua and LuaJIT come from Arch Linux packages linked through cgo, so their build flags are the distribution's, not stated in the README. Benchmark sizes are small (most Are We Fast Yet programs run one inner iteration; several rows take under 1 ms per op) and Go's benchmark loop amortizes JIT compilation, so the figures are steady-state. The M1 Pro table predates the Lua 5.5 port, compares against C Lua 5.4 and was run on a machine that was not idle (Apogee is 1.2x slower on binary-trees there). Very young: first release v1.0.0 on 2026-09-26 (bench runs from 2026-09-25); 540 commits including the inherited Shopify/go-lua history; most recent commits are co-authored by Claude and the README says generative AI did the engineering; 0 stars. Go, not C++. Found under its earlier repository name matjam/luart (renamed September 2026).

tier_reason: The README's current JIT_MATRIX (revision 8fa2a48, v0.12.11, measured 2026-09-30) carries every quoted number with 95% bootstrap intervals; the harness is public (benchmarks/run.rs built with 'cargo build --release --manifest-path benchmarks/Cargo.toml', benchmarks/paired.py, benchmarks/scripts/*.js) with raw process records and metadata JSON under benchmarks/results/, and rustc 1.98.1 / LLVM 22.1.8, the i7-13700KF (CPU 8 pinned, powersave) and the QuickJS-NG commit are stated, so A holds. The C compiler that builds the vendored QuickJS-NG is not named, but the interpreter control is the same binary with the JIT detached.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Against the same-revision QuickJS-NG interpreter (JIT detached), README matrix for 0.12.11: 18.3x-49.2x on the scalar, call, property and typed-array kernels (scalar-control-flow 49.2x, scalar-expressions 47.4x, fibonacci-iterative 45.8x, quickjs-bitops 42.6x, fibonacci-recursive 27.1x, float64-dense 22.2x, quickjs-int-arith 18.3x), smaller gains elsewhere (quickjs-fibonacci 2.5x, arrays-typed 2.2x, mixed-quotes 4.3x, objects-polymorphic 1.3x); 23 of 35 scenarios faster, 5 slower (collections 0.98x, strings-json 0.96x, json-codec 0.96x, map-set-bigint 0.99x, exceptions-promises-async 0.98x) and 7 tied, including strings-regexp, calls-closures and exceptions-sync. Slower than Bun 1.4.0 in all 35 scenarios (0.012x-0.73x of Bun's speed).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 15 stars, 1 fork; crate quickjs-jit on crates.io has 110 downloads and its latest published version is 0.12.6 (2026-09-03), so the measured 0.12.11 revision is available from git only
corrections.caveats: Same project as https://github.com/longbridge/quickjs-jit: the repository was renamed and longbridge/rquickjs now shows longbridge/quickjs-jit, which was already verified at tier A (wave 12 batch-45) and filed under jits. First-party harness, though raw process records, hashes and machine-readable comparisons are checked in. The baseline is the interpreter of the same engine, not a production JIT: every scenario is slower than Bun (JavaScriptCore). The 35 scenarios are the project's own micro-kernels, not a standard suite, and the protocol warms each process with 64 ten-call batches and polls the JIT outside the timed region, so tier-up latency and host-call overhead are not measured (the README says so). Gains are confined to numeric and scalar code; collections, JSON, strings, regexp and exceptions are unchanged or slightly slower than the interpreter. The previous release (0.12.10) regressed real gpui-shell renders and is fixed in the measured revision. The C compiler for the vendored QuickJS-NG is not named. Very new: crate first published 2026-09-01, crates.io stops at 0.12.6. Rust, not C++.

notes: Numbers, MIT licence, fork of DelSkayn/rquickjs, 15 stars and last commit 2026-09-30 verified. DUPLICATE: this id is the old URL of https://github.com/longbridge/quickjs-jit (GitHub shows the renamed repository), already confirmed A in batch-45 with a keep decision under jits; record decision duplicate for https://github.com/longbridge/rquickjs. Shortcomings: slower than Bun everywhere, only beats its own interpreter, project-written micro-kernels, measured revision not on crates.io.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the README's figures come from Xu and Kjolstad, 'Copy-and-Patch Compilation' (OOPSLA 2021, PACMPL vol. 5, article 136), a peer-reviewed paper by third-party authors, opened here from the author's checked-in PDF; its Fig. 18, 20 and 22 show Wasmtime 0.26 Cranelift against V8 TurboFan and WAVM (LLVM) on an Intel i7-7700HQ. Not A: no public benchmark harness or Wasm build flags were found, and Figs. 21-22 are averages of three runs without confidence intervals.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (citing the paper's Fig. 22): generated code about 2% slower than V8 TurboFan and about 14% slower than WAVM (LLVM); compilation about an order of magnitude faster than WAVM. Paper figures, read from the bar charts (approximate): PolyBenchC average execution time normalized to copy-and-patch 0.70 for Wasmtime Cranelift, 0.69 for V8 TurboFan and 0.61 for WAVM (Fig. 22); startup delay normalized to copy-and-patch about 105-110 for Wasmtime Cranelift against about 800-1150 for WAVM on CoreMark, PolyBenchC and clang.wasm, so roughly 7-10x faster compilation than LLVM (derived from page data), while V8 TurboFan compiled faster than Cranelift on CoreMark, PolyBenchC and clang.wasm (about 45-88) and tied on AutoCAD (Fig. 18); CoreMark 10000 iterations about 0.59 s for Wasmtime Cranelift, 0.94 s for TurboFan and 0.43 s for WAVM (Fig. 20).
corrections.workload: CoreMark 1.0 and the 30 PolyBenchC 4.2.1 kernels compiled to WebAssembly (execution time and startup delay), plus the AutoCAD (47.5 MB) and clang.wasm (30.5 MB) modules for code-generation time only; compilation limited to one CPU for every engine; Wasmtime 0.26 Cranelift against Chrome 81 V8 TurboFan, Wasmer 1.0 and WAVM (Figs. 17-22 of the paper).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Wasmtime 0.26 (Cranelift), Chrome 81 V8 (TurboFan selected with browser developer flags), Wasmer 1.0, WAVM (version not given); compilation single-threaded; the flags used to build the Wasm benchmark modules are not stated in the methodology section
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-7700HQ at 2.80 GHz, turbo on, 8 logical cores, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from a 2021 third-party paper (Xu and Kjolstad, Copy-and-Patch Compilation, OOPSLA 2021, arXiv 2011.13127) measuring Wasmtime 0.26; current Cranelift (0.137) differs, so the figures are dated. The runtime result is a loss: about 2% slower than V8 TurboFan and about 14% slower than WAVM (LLVM) on the PolyBenchC average, though on CoreMark Cranelift's code ran faster than TurboFan's. The only win is compile speed against LLVM (WAVM), and V8 TurboFan compiled faster than Cranelift on three of four modules, so against V8 Cranelift loses on both axes. Figs. 21-22 are averages of three runs without confidence intervals; WAVM never finished AutoCAD (LLVM dead loop). Ratios above are read from bar charts and approximate. Rust, not C++. rustc_codegen_cranelift (wave 2, compilers-frontends) is a separate catalogue entry that uses Cranelift as a rustc backend.

notes: README numbers match the cited paper, which is the copy-and-patch OOPSLA 2021 paper (arXiv blocked; opened from raw.githubusercontent.com/sillycross/sillycross.github.io/master/assets/copy-and-patch.pdf and checked Figs. 18, 20, 22), so tier goes C to B. Metadata verified: Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, 18.7k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, cranelift-codegen 51,595,493 crates.io downloads. Shortcomings: loses to V8 on code speed and compile speed, wins only compile speed against LLVM, numbers from Wasmtime 0.26 in 2021, three-run averages; not a duplicate (no other wasmtime entry in wave 12).
